new_statements.relation_note: new: nothing on record. First primary-source prosodic observations for Upper Umpqua held by the project, but they are token-level accent transcriptions plus two narrow generalizations, not a word-stress rule; the apparent stem-syllable prominence is my reading of the marked forms, not Harrington's claim. Thousands of further frames (reel 19 fr. ~10-300; reels 25-27 Box 65 'Grammatical Notes') remain unread and handwritten (no scanned).
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule is stated. Harrington transcribes accent token by token: an acute on the accented (loud, high) syllable, grave/breve marks or the label 'accentless' on unaccented syllables, a circumflex glossed 'long falling', and pitch labels ('app. high level', 'equally loud and high'). In the sampled paradigms the accent sits on the noun/verb stem syllable (cíic-lá' 'my hand', náan-lά' 'your hand', wαntɪ́ntcαk 'it hurts'), and he adds two limited generalizations: the final syllable of 3rd-person-plural possessed forms is 'often or usually accentless', and a theoretically long vowel is shortened 'under lack of accent'. That is evidence that he heard a syllable accent with pitch correlates in Upper Umpqua, not a statement of where word stress falls.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none stated; fr. 100 marks two syllables of 'óo lά' 'their hands' as 'equally loud and high'.
new_statements.exceptions: fr. 100: last syllable of 3 pl. possessed forms often/usually accentless (whereas sg. possessed 'hand' forms carry the accent on the stem -lá').
new_statements.identity_note: Upper Umpqua (Athabaskan of the upper Umpqua River, Oregon) as remembered in 1940 by John Warren at Grand Ronde, elicited by Harrington while rehearing Kwalhioqua-Tlatskanai and Frachtenberg vocabularies (slips headed 'UU'); Gatschet's 1877 MS 76 was likewise taken at Grand Ronde. Not Lower Umpqua (Kuitsh/Siuslawan), which is a different language (Milhau's MS 958).

sources.citation: Hale, Horatio. 1846. Ethnography and Philology. United States Exploring Expedition, vol. VI. Philadelphia. (Tahkali-Umkwa family notes; Umkwa vocabulary; orthography sec. 5)
sources.note: Only a general orthographic convention (acute accent marks 'those syllables on which the stress of voice falls') applying to all vocabularies; the Umkwa note says only that Umkwa is 'much softer than the others'. No statement of where Umpqua stress falls; accents in the wordlist are raw data only.

sources.citation: Scouler, John. 1841. Observations on the Indigenous Tribes of the N.W. Coast of America. Journal of the Royal Geographical Society of London 11: 215-251 (Tolmie's Umpqua vocabulary).
sources.note: Comparative vocabulary columns only; no remarks on accent or pronunciation.

sources.citation: Hall, Jaeci. 2021. Indigenous Methodologies in Linguistics: A Case Study of Nuu-wee-ya' Language Revitalization. Ph.D. dissertation, University of Oregon (Scholars' Bank 1794/26876).
sources.note: Upper Umpqua is mentioned (pp. 20, 32) only as a separate Oregon Dene language with 'minimal archival data', outside the Nuu-wee-ya' varieties described; no Upper Umpqua phonology; the word 'stress' does not occur in the dissertation.

sources.citation: Spence, Justin. 2013. Language Change, Contact, and Koineization in Pacific Coast Athabaskan. Ph.D. dissertation, University of California, Berkeley. eScholarship item 7rm5p5nw. Ch. 2 Appendix C 'The Status of Upper Umpqua', pp. 70-76.
sources.note: Nothing on stress placement in Upper Umpqua. Appendix C.2 (p. 72) treats only segmental sound changes and says Upper Umpqua 'appears to lack lexical tone, or at any rate retains coda laryngeal segments that develop into tone elsewhere in Athabaskan'; fn. 37: Harrington's notes suggest 'incipient quasi-tonal phenomena in Upper Umpqua, but this remains to be explored'. The word 'stress' occurs only in the Hupa/English-loan chapter.

sources.note: The standard modern reference on PCA documentation; Spence quotes it as noting Upper Umpqua's 'distinctive lexical and phonological features'. It is the only published synthesis likely to carry any remark on Upper Umpqua (or general Oregon Athabaskan) prosody; needs checking even though it is probably silent on stress.

sources.note: Comparative stem-initial consonants only; states 'none of the Pacific Coast languages so far studied possess tone phonemes' and cites 'the absence of pitch accent in PCA'; nothing on stress placement in Umpqua.
